chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Al-Hakam ibn Miskeen, from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

There was a king among the Children of Israel, and he had a judge, and the judge had a brother who was a man of truth. He had a wife who had been given birth to by the Prophets (peace be upon them). The king wanted to send a man for a need, so he said to the judge, 'Find me a reliable man.' He said, 'I do not know anyone more reliable than my brother.' So he called him to send him, but that man disliked it and said to his brother, 'I dislike that I should lose my wife.' He was determined upon it, so he could not find a way out but to go out. He said to his brother, 'O my brother! I am not leaving behind anything more worrying upon me than my wife, so stay in her place and manage her affairs.' He said, 'Yes.'

So the man went out, and the wife had disliked his going out. So the judge used to come to her and ask her about her needs and attend to her. He became fascinated with her, so he invited her to himself, but she refused. He swore to her, 'If you do not do it, I will surely inform the king that you have been immoral.' She said, 'Do whatever you like; I will not respond to you to anything from what you seek.'

So he went to the king and said, 'The wife of my brother has been immoral, and that is a right with me.' The king said to him, 'Purify her.' So he came to her and said, 'The king has ordered me to stone you. What are you saying? Respond to me, or else I will stone you.' She said, 'I will not respond to you, so do whatever you like.' So he brought her out, dug a pit for her, and stoned her, and the people were with him.

When he thought that she had died, he left her and turned away. Night came upon her, and there was still some breath in her. So she moved and came out of the pit. Then she walked on her face until she came out of the city and reached a monastery wherein was a monk. She slept at the door of the monastery. When it was morning, the monk opened the door and saw her. He asked her about her story, and she informed him. He pitied her and entered her into the monastery. He had a young son, and he did not have a son other than him, and he was of good condition.

He treated her until she was cured from her illness and healed. Then he handed over his son to her, and she used to raise him. The monk had a manager who attended to his affairs. He was fascinated with her and invited her to himself, but she refused. He struggled with her, but she still refused. He said, 'If you do not do it, I will strive to kill you.' She said, 'Do whatever you like.' So he went to the young boy and broke his neck. He came to the monk and said to him, 'You took an immoral woman who had been immoral, and you handed over your son to her, and she killed him.'

So the monk came, and when he saw her, he said to her, 'What is this? And you know what I have done for you.' So she informed him with the story. He said to her, 'I am not pleased that you should be with me, so get out.' So he threw her out at night and handed over twenty dirhams to her and said to her, 'Take this as provision; Allah is sufficient for you.'

So she went out at night, and in the morning she was in a town. There was a man crucified on a wooden cross, and he was alive. She asked about his story, and they said, 'Upon him is a debt of twenty dirhams. And whoever has a debt with us for his companion, he is crucified until he pays it to his companion.' So she brought out the twenty dirhams and handed them to his creditor and said, 'Do not kill him.' So they brought him down from the wooden cross. He said to her, 'No one is greater to me in favor than you. You saved me from the crucifixion and from death. So I am with you wherever you go.'

So he went with her, and she went until they reached the coast of the sea. He saw a group of people and ships, so he said to her, 'Sit until I go and work for them and get food and bring it to you.' So he went to them and said to them, 'What is in this ship of yours?' They said, 'In this are merchandise, jewels, amber, and things of trade. And as for this, we are in it.' He said, 'And how much is what is in your ship?' They said, 'A lot, we cannot count it.' He said, 'But with me is something that is better than what is in your ship.' They said, 'And what is with you?' He said, 'A slave girl whom you have never seen the like of.' They said, 'So sell her to us.' He said, 'Yes, on the condition that one of you goes and looks at her, then comes to me and buys her, and does not inform her, and hands over the price to me, and does not inform her until I go away.' They said, 'That is for you.'

So they sent someone to look at her, and he said, 'I have not seen the like of her.' So they bought her from him for ten thousand dirhams and handed the dirhams to him. So he went away with her. When he was at a distance, they came to her and said to her, 'Stand up and enter the ship.' She said, 'And why?' They said, 'We have bought you from your master.' She said, 'He is not my master.' They said, 'Either you stand up or we will carry you.' So she stood up and went with them.

When they reached the coast, they did not trust each other over her, so they put her in the ship that had the jewels and merchandise, and they themselves boarded the other ship and pushed it. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent winds upon them which drowned them and their ship. The ship in which she was was saved until it reached an island from the islands of the sea. She tied the ship and circled around in the island. There was water therein, and trees with fruit. She said, 'This is water I shall drink from, and fruit I shall eat from. I will worship Allah in this place.'

So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to a Prophet from the Prophets of the Children of Israel that he should go to that king and say, 'In an island from the islands of the sea, there is a creature from My creatures. So go out, you and those in your kingdom, until you come to this creature of Mine, and confess to her your sins. Then ask that creature to seek forgiveness for you. If she seeks forgiveness for you, I will forgive you.'

So the king went out with the people of his kingdom to that island, and they saw a woman. The king proceeded to her and said to her, 'This judge of mine came to me and informed me that the wife of his brother had been immoral, so I ordered him to stone her, and he did not establish the proof in my presence. Thus, I fear that I may have proceeded upon what is not permissible for me. I would love it if you seek forgiveness for me.' She said, 'Allah has forgiven you. Sit.'

Then her husband came, and he did not recognize her. He said, 'There used to be a wife for me, and she was from the meritorious and righteous ones. I went out from her, and she disliked that. So I left my brother in charge over her. When I returned, I asked about her, and my brother informed me that she had been immoral, so he stoned her. And I fear that I may have lost her. So seek forgiveness for me.' She said, 'Allah has forgiven you. Sit.'

So she seated him next to the king. Then the judge came and said, 'There used to be a wife of my brother, and she astounded me. So I invited her to immorality, but she refused. So I informed the king that she had been immoral, and he ordered me to stone her. So I stoned her, and I was lying about her. So seek forgiveness for me.' She said, 'Allah has forgiven you.'

Then she turned to her husband and said, 'Listen.' Then the monk proceeded and related his story and said, 'I threw her out at night, and I fear that a beast may have met her and killed her.' She said, 'Allah has forgiven you. Sit.'
Then the manager proceeded and related his story. She said to the monk, 'Listen. Allah has forgiven you.'
Then the crucified one proceeded and related his story. She said, 'No, Allah will not forgive you.'

He said, 'Then she turned to her husband and said, 'I am your wife, and everything you have heard is my story. I have no need of the men, and I would love it if you take this ship and what is in it, and free my way, so I can worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in this island, for you have seen what I have faced from the men.' So he did it and took the ship and what was in it, and freed her way. And the king and the people of his kingdom turned away.'
ai.seo_question: What is the story of the stoned woman in Surah al-Kafi who granted forgiveness to the King of Israel?
ai.summary: This narrative from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia concept of *al-istidraj* (gradual divine ensnarement) and the accumulation of sins through false testimony, where the judge's brother's lie leads to the stoning of the righteous woman. The story highlights the spiritual hierarchy of forgiveness, as the woman grants pardon to those who sought it with humility (the King, husband, monk, manager) while withholding it from the arrogant debtor, demonstrating that divine mercy is often mediated through the intercession of the righteous. It serves as a practical lesson on the consequences of false accusations and the power of *maghfira* (forgiveness) in restoring social and spiritual order.
